subject: social_sciences
chapter_title: Chapter 4: Timeline and Sources of History

competencies.justification: The section 'What Are the Sources of History?' is built around collecting and interpreting multiple sources to understand historical aspects of human life. It taxonomises source types (archaeological, inscriptional, oral, literary, foreign accounts, artistic), explains how historians cross-check sources and adjudicate contradictions, and sets a student activity examining real artefacts to infer historical information. The chapter would have no purpose without it. This is the chapter's central focus because 'Sources of History' appears in the chapter title, in the opening Big Question ('How can various sources help us understand history?') and in the first defined term ('source of history'), and dominates the exercises and project at the chapter's end.

The section 'How Is Time Measured in History?' is self-contained; its central activity is representing and analysing historical data in timeline form — exactly what C-1.2 requires. The section introduces the CE/BCE system, century and millennium units, and includes two 'Let's Explore' activity blocks where students construct personal timelines and perform date calculations by reading/building chronological diagrams. This section is self-contained. C-1.2 is treated as a major strand because C-1.1 more completely occupies the chapter's primary organising purpose as evidenced by the exercise set and chapter title order.

Two consecutive sections — 'The Beginnings of Human History' and 'The First Crops' — trace a full causal arc: from early Homo sapiens as hunter-gatherers (rock shelters, stone tools, rock paintings) through the post-Ice Age transition to settled life, the emergence of agriculture and animal domestication, changes in habitation (hamlets to villages to towns), evolving social structures (chieftains, collective ownership, community welfare), and new basic technologies (pottery, copper and iron metallurgy). The chapter joins the two sections as a continuous arc ending with the note that this 'prepared for the emergence of civilisation' (Chapter 6). It runs as a deliberate thread through several sections, with the chapter making that continuity evident.

One part of the chapter — the 'Think About It' box within 'The First Crops' section — takes as its subject the assumed gender roles depicted in early human rock shelter and agricultural scenes. It notes that these depictions 'may appear to be natural' but 'are not necessarily accurate and do not cover all situations', offers counter-examples (women painting rock art, men cooking or caring for children), and asks students to think and discuss these roles critically. That requires students to identify and question gender-based assumptions in their historical context. It is a part of the chapter whose subject is this competency, but not a dedicated section or self-contained activity block.
